concepts: Roots of a polynomial equation reducible to a cubic in $x^2$, ordered by modulus
questions.question: Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_7$ be the roots of the equation $x^7+3x^5-13x^3-15x=0$ and $|\alpha_1|\ge|\alpha_2|\ge\ldots\ge|\alpha_7|$. Then $\alpha_1\alpha_2-\alpha_3\alpha_4+\alpha_5\alpha_6$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The polynomial is odd, so $x=0$ is a root and the rest depend only on $t=x^2$, giving a cubic in $t$ whose roots are $3,-1,-5$.
solution: Moduli in decreasing order: $\sqrt5,\sqrt5,\sqrt3,\sqrt3,1,1,0$, so $\alpha_{1,2}=\pm\sqrt5 i$, $\alpha_{3,4}=\pm\sqrt3$, $\alpha_{5,6}=\pm i$, $\alpha_7=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each pair $\pm\beta$ has product $-\beta^2=-t$, so the expression is $-t_a+t_b-t_c$ in terms of the roots of the cubic; Vieta then needs only the one rational root.
solution: Roots come in pairs $\pm\beta$ with $\beta^2=t$, and the product of a pair is $\beta(-\beta)=-t$.
Rational root test: $t=3$ gives $27+27-39-15=0$, so $3$ is a root.
The other two roots have sum $-3-3=-6$ and product $\frac{15}{3}=5$, so both are negative: $t=-1$ and $t=-5$.
The moduli are $\sqrt{|t|}$, so in decreasing order the pairs are $t=-5$, then $t=3$, then $t=-1$.

useful_results: An odd polynomial $x\,g(x^2)$ has the root $0$ and its other roots come in pairs $\pm\beta$ with $\beta^2$ a root of $g$.
The product of the pair $\pm\beta$ is $-\beta^2$; for a negative $t$ (imaginary pair $\pm\sqrt{|t|}\,i$) this is $+|t|$, for a positive $t$ it is $-t$.
Rational root test: for monic integer polynomials try the divisors of the constant term (here $\pm1,\pm3,\pm5,\pm15$); one root then reduces the cubic to a quadratic.
Ties in modulus (such as $\sqrt5,\sqrt5$) do not matter when the expression multiplies the two members of the tied pair.

concepts: Sum of an arithmetic progression (numbers with a given remainder)
questions.question: The sum of all two digit positive numbers which when divided by $7$ yield $2$ or $5$ as remainder is :
questions.key_idea: Numbers with remainder $r$ on division by $7$ form an AP of common difference $7$; list only the two-digit members (first term $16$ and $12$).
solution: Two-digit numbers leaving remainder $2$ on division by $7$ form the AP $16,23,30,\ldots,93$ ($9$ is one digit); it has $12$ terms.
Two-digit numbers leaving remainder $5$ form the AP $12,19,26,\ldots,96$; it has $13$ terms.
The two classes are disjoint, so the required sum is $654+702=1356$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF lists the first AP as '2 + 9 + ... + 91 = 654' and the second as '5 + 12 + ... + 94 = 702'. These lists are wrong (2 and 9 are not two-digit; 91 and 94 are not of the form 7k+2 / 7k+5, and the sum of the first list as printed would be 651, not 654). The totals 654 and 702 are right for the correct lists 16..93 (12 terms) and 12..96 (13 terms); the working was rewritten with the correct lists and term counts. Final answer 1356 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Group the numbers in blocks $7k,\dots,7k+6$: each block contributes the pair $7k+2$ and $7k+5$ with sum $14k+7$.
solution: Block $k$ (numbers $7k$ to $7k+6$) holds exactly one number with remainder $2$ and one with remainder $5$: $7k+2$ and $7k+5$, with sum $14k+7$.
For $k=2,\ldots,13$ both numbers are two-digit ($16,19$ up to $93,96$).
For $k=1$: $7+2=9$ is one digit, but $7+5=12$ is two-digit, so add $12$.
For $k=14$ the numbers $100,\ldots$ exceed two digits; for $k=0$ both are one digit.

useful_results: Numbers $\equiv r\pmod m$ in a range form an AP of common difference $m$; the count is $\frac{\text{last}-\text{first}}{m}+1$ and the sum is $\frac{n}{2}(\text{first}+\text{last})$.
Always take the first term from inside the range (here $16$, not $2$ or $9$): a wrong first term changes the term count.
Pairing the two residue classes block by block turns the sum into one AP in $k$: $\sum(14k+7)$.
Check: $654=12\times54.5$ and $702=13\times54$ (mean of an AP is its middle term, mean of first and last).

concepts: General term of an arithmetic progression
questions.question: If $19^{\text{th}}$ term of a non-zero A.P. is zero, then its ($49^{\text{th}}$ term) : ($29^{\text{th}}$ term) is :
questions.key_idea: $a_{19}=0$ gives $a=-18d$, so every term is a multiple of $d$.
solution: $\frac{T_{49}}{T_{29}}=\frac{30d}{10d}=3$, i.e. the ratio is $3:1$ (here $d\neq0$, since the A.P. is non-zero and its $19^{\text{th}}$ term is zero).

alternate_solutions.idea: The $n^{\text{th}}$ term is a linear function of $n$ vanishing at $n=19$, so $T_n=d\,(n-19)$.
solution: The ratio is $\frac{49-19}{29-19}=\frac{30}{10}=3$; the same answer.

useful_results: If $T_p=0$ in an A.P. then $T_n=d(n-p)$ and $T_m:T_n=(m-p):(n-p)$.
Two terms of an A.P. of the same sign on either side of the zero term are in the ratio of their distances from it.

concepts: Quadratic equation with trigonometric coefficients
Sum of an infinite geometric progression
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the quadratic equation $x^2\sin\theta-x(\sin\theta\cos\theta+1)+\cos\theta=0$ $(0<\theta<45^\circ)$, and $\alpha<\beta$. Then $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\alpha^n+\frac{(-1)^n}{\beta^n}\right)$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: The roots are $\cos\theta$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$, and $0<\theta<45^\circ$ gives $\alpha=\cos\theta<\beta$, and both series ratios $\cos\theta,-\sin\theta$ lie in $(-1,1)$.

solution: The product of the roots is $\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$, so the other root is $\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$.
Numerical check at $\theta=0.3$ rad: 300 terms of the series sum to $23.1615$ and option (D) gives $23.1615$.

useful_results: $\sum_{n\ge0}r^n=\frac{1}{1-r}$ for $|r|<1$; hence $\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^n}{\beta^n}=\frac{1}{1+1/\beta}=\frac{\beta}{\beta+1}$ when $|\beta|>1$.

A quadratic with trigonometric coefficients is often a product of two linear factors: $\sin\theta\,x^2-(1+\sin\theta\cos\theta)x+\cos\theta=(x-\cos\theta)(x\sin\theta-1)$. Look for the pattern $ax^2-(ab+1)x+b=(x-b)(ax-1)$.
The ordering condition $\alpha<\beta$ decides which root goes to $\alpha$; on $(0,45^\circ)$, $\cos\theta<1<\operatorname{cosec}\theta$.
A series $\sum(p^n+q^n)$ converges iff $|p|<1$ and $|q|<1$; here $|{\cos\theta}|<1$ and $|\sin\theta|<1$.

concepts: AM-GM inequality (greatest value of an expression)
questions.question: Let $x,y$ be positive real numbers and $m,n$ positive integers. The maximum value of the expression $\frac{x^my^n}{(1+x^{2m})(1+y^{2n})}$ is :
questions.key_idea: Divide each factor by $x^m$ (resp. $y^n$) to get $t+\frac1t\ge2$ in both denominators.
solution: Divide numerator and denominator by $x^my^n$: expression $=\frac{1}{\left(\frac1{x^m}+x^m\right)}\times\frac{1}{\left(\frac1{y^n}+y^n\right)}$.
Both factors are positive, so their product is $\le\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$.
Equality holds at $x=y=1$, so the maximum value is $\frac14$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x^m=\tan u$, $y^n=\tan v$: then $\frac{x^m}{1+x^{2m}}=\sin u\cos u=\frac12\sin2u$.
solution: Equality when $u=v=\frac\pi4$, i.e. $x=y=1$; the maximum is $\frac14$, same answer.

useful_results: For $t>0$: $\frac{t}{1+t^2}\le\frac12$ with equality at $t=1$ (since $t+\frac1t\ge2$); the substitution $t=\tan u$ gives $\frac12\sin2u$.
The bound is independent of the exponents $m,n$ because $x^m$ is just another positive number $t$.
The bounds of two positive factors can be multiplied; equality needs both to attain their bounds simultaneously (here at $x=y=1$).

concepts: Sum of cubes of the first $n$ natural numbers
questions.question: If the sum of the first $15$ terms of the series $\left(\frac34\right)^3+\left(1\frac12\right)^3+\left(2\frac14\right)^3+3^3+\left(3\frac34\right)^3+\ldots$ is equal to $225k$, then $k$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The bases $\frac34,\frac64,\frac94,\frac{12}4,\frac{15}4,\ldots$ equal $\frac{3r}{4}$, so the sum is $\frac{27}{64}\sum r^3$.
solution: The terms are $\left(\frac{3\cdot1}{4}\right)^3,\left(\frac{3\cdot2}{4}\right)^3,\left(\frac{3\cdot3}{4}\right)^3,\ldots$, i.e. the $r^{\text{th}}$ term is $\left(\frac{3r}{4}\right)^3=\frac{27}{64}r^3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cancel the squares first: $\frac{120^2}{64\cdot225}=\left(\frac{120}{8\cdot15}\right)^2=1$, so only $27$ survives.
solution: Sum $=\frac{27}{64}\cdot120^2$ and we need this $=225k$, so $k=\frac{27\cdot120^2}{64\cdot225}$.
$8\cdot15=120$, so the bracket is $1$ and $k=27$; the same answer.

useful_results: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^3=\left(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\right)^2=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$; for $n=15$ it is $120^2$.
Spot the pattern in mixed numbers: $\frac34,1\frac12,2\frac14,3,3\frac34$ are equally spaced (common difference $\frac34$), so the base is $\frac{3r}{4}$.
Constants come out of power sums: $\sum(cr)^3=c^3\sum r^3$.

concepts: Geometric and arithmetic progressions
questions.question: The product of three consecutive terms of a G.P. is $512$. If $4$ is added to each of the first and the second of these terms, the three terms now form an A.P. Then the sum of the original three terms of the given G.P. is :
questions.key_idea: Write the G.P. terms as $\frac ar,a,ar$; the product gives the middle term $a=8$ at once.
solution: Let the three consecutive terms be $\frac ar,\ a,\ ar$.
The terms are $\frac8r,\ 8,\ 8r$. Adding $4$ to the first and second: $\frac8r+4,\ 12,\ 8r$.
These are in A.P., so their sum is $3\times12=36$: $\frac8r+4+12+8r=36$, i.e. $\frac8r+8r=20$.
(The PDF writes this as $\frac8r+4+8r=24$, the same relation.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $r$ explicitly and list the actual terms, then check the A.P.
solution: After adding $4$ to the first two terms: $8,12,16$, an A.P. with common difference $4$. Valid.
For $r=\frac12$ the G.P. is $16,8,4$; the modified list is $20,12,4$, an A.P. with common difference $-8$. Also valid.
In both cases the sum is $4+8+16=28$; the same answer.

useful_results: Three consecutive terms of a G.P.: take $\frac ar,a,ar$; their product is $a^3$, the middle term is the cube root of the product.
Three terms in A.P. have sum equal to $3\times$ (middle term).
The condition is symmetric under $r\to\frac1r$ (reversing the G.P.), so both reciprocal ratios give the same sum, $28$.

concepts: Sum of squares of natural numbers
questions.question: Let $S_k=\frac{1+2+3+\ldots+k}{k}$. If $S_1^2+S_2^2+\ldots+S_{10}^2=\frac{5}{12}A$, then $A$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $1+2+\ldots+k=\frac{k(k+1)}2$ makes $S_k=\frac{k+1}{2}$, so $\sum S_k^2=\frac14\sum(k+1)^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $(k+1)^2=k^2+2k+1$ and use three standard sums instead of shifting the index.
solution: So $\sum S_k^2=\frac{505}{4}$ and $\frac5{12}A=\frac{505}4$ gives $A=\frac{505\times12}{4\times5}=303$; the same answer.

useful_results: The mean of $1,2,\ldots,k$ is $\frac{k+1}2$ (middle of the list), so $\frac{1+2+\ldots+k}{k}=\frac{k+1}{2}$.
When an index is shifted ($j=k+1$) the limits move: $k=1..10\to j=2..11$; subtract the missing $j=1$ term.

concepts: Geometric and arithmetic progressions
questions.question: Let $a,b$ and $c$ be the $7^{\text{th}},11^{\text{th}}$ and $13^{\text{th}}$ terms respectively of a non-constant A.P. If these are also the three consecutive terms of a G.P., then $\frac ac$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Three consecutive G.P. terms satisfy $b^2=ac$; write each term through the first term $a_1$ and $d$ and the first term cancels to $a_1=-14d$.
solution: Let the A.P. have first term $A$ and common difference $d\neq0$ (the PDF calls the first term $a$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the middle term $b=T_{11}$ as the base: $a=b-4d$, $c=b+2d$.
solution: Then $a=-8d$, $c=-2d$ and $\frac ac=4$; the same answer.
Interpretation: the G.P. has common ratio $\frac ba=\frac12$, so $\frac ac=\left(\frac ab\right)^2=4$.

useful_results: If $a,b,c$ are in G.P. with ratio $q$ then $\frac ac=\frac1{q^2}$.
Parametrising an A.P. around the middle given term ($b\pm kd$) removes the unknown first term.
For a non-constant A.P. whose terms $T_p,T_q,T_r$ are in G.P.: $T_q=-\frac{(p-q)(r-q)}{p+r-2q}\,d$; here $p,q,r=7,11,13$ gives $T_{11}=-4d$.
Check with $d=1$: $T_7=-8$, $T_{11}=-4$, $T_{13}=-2$ is a G.P. with ratio $\frac12$.

concepts: Sum of $n$ terms of a series using sums of squares and cubes
questions.question: The sum of the following series $1+6+\frac{9\left(1^2+2^2+3^2\right)}{7}+\frac{12\left(1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2\right)}{9}+\frac{15\left(1^2+2^2+\ldots+5^2\right)}{11}+\ldots$ up to $15$ terms, is :
questions.key_idea: Reading the pattern, $T_n=\frac{3n\,(1^2+\cdots+n^2)}{2n+1}$ collapses to $\frac12(n^3+n^2)$.
solution: The $n^{\text{th}}$ term is $T_n=\frac{3n\left(1^2+2^2+\ldots+n^2\right)}{2n+1}$ (check: $n=1$ gives $1$, $n=2$ gives $6$, $n=3$ gives $\frac{9\cdot14}{7}$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $n^2(n+1)=n(n+1)(n+2)-2n(n+1)$ and sum the products of consecutive integers by the telescoping rule.

useful_results: $1^2+2^2+\ldots+n^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$; the factor $(2n+1)$ in the denominator is designed to cancel.
Telescoping rule: $\sum_{n=1}^{N}n(n+1)\cdots(n+k-1)=\frac{N(N+1)\cdots(N+k)}{k+1}$.
Find a general term from the first few terms: here the multiplier $3,6,9,\ldots=3n$ and the denominators $3,5,7,\ldots=2n+1$ (the first term $1=\frac{3\cdot1}{3}$).

concepts: Sum of an arithmetic progression
questions.question: Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{30}$ be an A.P., $S=\sum_{i=1}^{30}a_i$ and $T=\sum_{i=1}^{15}a_{(2i-1)}$. If $a_5=27$ and $S-2T=75$, then $a_{10}$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: Write $S$ and $T$ with the sum formula; $2a+29d$ and $2a+28d$ differ by $d$, so $S-2T=15d$.
solution: $T=a_1+a_3+\ldots+a_{29}$ is an A.P. of $15$ terms with first term $a$ and common difference $2d$: $T=\frac{15}{2}\left(2a+14\times2d\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The sum of an A.P. is (number of terms) $\times$ (middle term); $T$ uses the odd-position terms, whose middle is $a_{15}$.
solution: $S=a_1+\ldots+a_{30}=15(a_{15}+a_{16})$ (pair first with last: every pair sums to $a_{15}+a_{16}$).
$T=a_1+a_3+\ldots+a_{29}$ is symmetric about $a_{15}$ (its middle term), so $T=15\,a_{15}$.

useful_results: For an A.P. with an odd number of terms, the sum is $n\times$ the middle term.
Terms at odd positions $a_1,a_3,a_5,\ldots$ form an A.P. with common difference $2d$.
Shortcut: $a_{10}=a_5+5d$.

concepts: Geometric progression
Real roots of a quadratic equation (discriminant)
questions.question: If $a,b$ and $c$ be three distinct real numbers in G.P. and $a+b+c=xb$, then $x$ cannot be:
questions.key_idea: With $a=\frac br,c=br$ we get $x=1+r+\frac1r$, and $r+\frac1r$ never lies in $(-2,2)$ for real $r$.
solution: Let the common ratio be $r$ and write $b=ar$, $c=ar^2$. Then $a+ar^2=ar(x-1)$.
The numbers are distinct, so $r\neq1$ (and $r\neq-1$, which would make $a=c$).
$r$ is real, so the discriminant $(1-x)^2-4\ge0$, i.e. $x^2-2x-3\ge0$, i.e. $x\le-1$ or $x\ge3$.
At $x=3$ the only root is $r=1$ and at $x=-1$ the only root is $r=-1$, both excluded, so in fact $x<-1$ or $x>3$.
Hence $x$ cannot lie in $[-1,3]$; of the options only $x=2$ lies there. $x$ cannot be $2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF says 'r != 1, so x != 2'. That implication is wrong: r = 1 corresponds to x = 3 (since x = 1 + r + 1/r), not x = 2. The correct reasoning is the discriminant condition (1-x)^2 - 4 >= 0, which the PDF also writes, giving x <= -1 or x >= 3 (with the end values excluded by distinctness); x = 2 is excluded because it lies in (-1, 3). Final answer (C) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $a$ and $c$ as the two roots of a quadratic with sum $(x-1)b$ and product $b^2$; they are real and distinct only if $(x-1)^2>4$.
solution: $a+c=(x-1)b$ and $ac=b^2$ (G.P.). So $a,c$ are the roots of $t^2-(x-1)b\,t+b^2=0$.
Test the option $x=2$ directly: $t^2-bt+b^2=0$ has discriminant $b^2-4b^2=-3b^2<0$ for $b\neq0$, so $a,c$ would not be real.
Check that the other options are possible: $x=4$ gives $t^2-3bt+b^2=0$ with discriminant $5b^2>0$; $x=-3$: $t^2+4bt+b^2$, discriminant $12b^2>0$; $x=-2$: $t^2+3bt+b^2$, discriminant $5b^2>0$.
In general real distinct $a,c$ need $(x-1)^2>4$, i.e. $x<-1$ or $x>3$. The same answer, $x\neq2$.

useful_results: For a G.P. $\frac br,b,br$: $\frac{a+b+c}{b}=1+r+\frac1r$, and $r+\frac1r\ge2$ if $r>0$, $\le-2$ if $r<0$.
Hence the ratio $\frac{a+b+c}{b}$ of a real G.P. lies in $(-\infty,-1]\cup[3,\infty)$, with $3$ and $-1$ only for the degenerate ratios $r=1,-1$.
Pairs $(a,c)$ with given sum $s$ and product $p$ are real iff $s^2\ge4p$: use it to bound parameters.
Instance: $x=1+r+\frac1r=3$ at $r=1$ and $-1$ at $r=-1$; $x=2$ would need $r+\frac1r=1$, impossible.

concepts: Divisibility and HCF (inclusion-exclusion)
Sum of an arithmetic progression
questions.question: The sum of all natural numbers $n$ such that $100<n<200$ and H.C.F.$(91,n)>1$ is :
questions.key_idea: $91=7\times13$, so $\mathrm{HCF}(91,n)>1$ exactly when $n$ is divisible by $7$ or $13$; use inclusion-exclusion on the sums.
solution: $91=13\times7$, so $\mathrm{HCF}(91,n)>1$ iff $n$ is divisible by $7$ or by $13$.
Sum of such $n$ = (sum of multiples of $7$) + (sum of multiples of $13$) $-$ (sum of multiples of $91$).
useful_results: $\mathrm{HCF}(m,n)>1$ for $m=pq$ (distinct primes) iff $p\mid n$ or $q\mid n$; the union's sum is $\Sigma_p+\Sigma_q-\Sigma_{pq}$.

Multiples of $k$ in $(L,U)$ form an A.P.: the count is $\left\lfloor\frac{U-1}{k}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\right\rfloor$ for the open range $L<n<U$, then use $\frac{\text{count}}{2}(\text{first}+\text{last})$.
Instance: counts $14,8,1$; $14+8-1=21$ numbers in all, with average $\frac{3121}{21}\approx148.6$ near the midpoint $150$.
Check at the ends: the range is open, so $100$ and $200$ are excluded (neither is a multiple of $7$ or $13$ anyway).

concepts: Geometric progression
Common root of two quadratic equations
questions.question: If three distinct numbers $a,b,c$ are in G.P. and the equations $ax^2+2bx+c=0$ and $dx^2+2ex+f=0$ have a common root, then which one of the following statements is correct ?
options: $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc$ are in G.P.
$\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc$ are in A.P.
questions.answer: (C) $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc$ are in A.P.
questions.key_idea: $b^2=ac$ makes $ax^2+2bx+c$ a perfect square with the double root $-\frac ba$; the common root must therefore be $-\frac ba$.
solution: $ax^2+2bx+c=0$ has discriminant $4b^2-4ac=0$, so it has a repeated root $x=-\frac ba$. (The PDF writes it as $a\left(x+\sqrt{c/a}\right)^2$ with root $-\sqrt{\frac ca}$, which presumes $b>0$.)
This is the only root of the first equation, so it must satisfy $dx^2+2ex+f=0$.
Divide by $c$: $\frac da-\frac{2eb}{ac}+\frac fc=0$, and $ac=b^2$ gives $\frac da-\frac{2e}{b}+\frac fc=0$.
So $\frac da+\frac fc=\frac{2e}{b}$, i.e. $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc$ are in A.P., option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF takes b = +sqrt(ac) (writes 2b x = 2 sqrt(ac) x and the root as -sqrt(c/a)), which silently assumes b > 0. If b < 0 the double root is +sqrt(c/a), not -sqrt(c/a). The result d/a + f/c = 2e/b still holds in both cases because the common root is -b/a. The working here is rewritten with the double root -b/a. Final answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the G.P. by its ratio: $(a,b,c)=(a,ar,ar^2)$, so the first equation is $a(x+r)^2=0$ with root $-r$ (valid for any sign of $r$).
solution: Now $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc=\frac da,\frac e{ar},\frac f{ar^2}=\frac1{ar^2}\left(dr^2,\ er,\ f\right)$.
These are in A.P. iff $2er=dr^2+f$, which is exactly the relation $dr^2-2er+f=0$ found above.
So $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc$ are in A.P.; the same answer, (C).
Numerical check: $a=1,r=2$ ($1,2,4$); take $d=1$, $e=\frac32$, $f=2$ (so $4-6+2=0$): $\frac da,\frac eb,\frac fc=1,\frac34,\frac12$, an A.P. with difference $-\frac14$.

useful_results: $ax^2+2bx+c$ with $b^2=ac$ is $a\left(x+\frac ba\right)^2$: a G.P. of coefficients means a repeated root $-\frac ba$.
A common root of two quadratics, one of which has a repeated root, is that repeated root: substitute it into the other.
Parametrising a G.P. by its ratio ($a,ar,ar^2$) handles all signs and avoids square roots.
Generalisation: for $ax^2+2bx+c$ with $b^2=ac$ and any $dx^2+2ex+f$ sharing a root, $\frac da-\frac{2e}b+\frac fc=0$.

concepts: Sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression and its common difference
questions.question: Let the sum of the first $n$ terms of a non constant A.P., $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ be $50n+\frac{n(n-7)}{2}A$, where $A$ is a constant. If $d$ is the common difference of this A.P., then the ordered pair $(d,a_{50})$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $S_n=\frac d2n^2+\left(a-\frac d2\right)n$, so the $n^2$ coefficient is $\frac d2$.
solution: For an A.P., $S_n=\frac d2n^2+\left(a_1-\frac d2\right)n$, so comparing the $n^2$ coefficient: $\frac d2=\frac A2$, giving $d=A$.
So $a_n=50+A(n-4)$, a linear function of $n$ with slope $A$: $d=A$.

useful_results: If $S_n=pn^2+qn$ then the sequence is an A.P. with $d=2p$ and $a_1=p+q$; a constant term in $S_n$ would break this (except $S_0=0$).
$a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ for $n\ge2$ and $a_1=S_1$ always gives the general term.
Instance: $p=\frac A2$, $q=50-\frac{7A}2$, so $d=A$ and $a_1=p+q=50-3A$.

concepts: Triangular numbers (sum of first $n$ natural numbers)
Quadratic equation
questions.question: Some identical balls are arranged in rows to form an equilateral triangle. The first row consists of one ball, the second row consists of two balls and so on. If $99$ more identical balls are added to the total number of balls used in forming the equilateral triangle, then all these balls can be arranged in a square whose each side contains exactly $2$ balls less than the number of balls each side of the triangle contains. Then the number of balls used to form the equilateral triangle is :
questions.key_idea: A triangle with $n$ balls on a side holds $\frac{n(n+1)}2$ balls, giving $\frac{n(n+1)}2+99=(n-2)^2$.
solution: Let each side of the triangle have $n$ balls. Balls in the triangle $=1+2+\ldots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$.
The square has $n-2$ balls on each side, so it holds $(n-2)^2$ balls.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the options: the number of balls must be a triangular number, and only $190$ is one.
solution: A triangle number $T=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ satisfies $8T+1=(2n+1)^2$, a perfect square.
Check the second condition: $190+99=289=17^2$ and $n-2=17$. The same answer, $190$.

useful_results: A positive integer $T$ is triangular iff $8T+1$ is a perfect square; then $n=\frac{\sqrt{8T+1}-1}{2}$.
Setting a triangular number plus a constant equal to a perfect square leads to a quadratic in the side $n$; always reject the negative root.
Check the geometric condition at the end: the square side $n-2=17$ is positive.

concepts: Sum of $n$ terms of a series using sums of powers of natural numbers
questions.question: The sum $\frac{3\cdot1^3}{1^2}+\frac{5\cdot(1^3+2^3)}{1^2+2^2}+\frac{7\cdot(1^3+2^3+3^3)}{1^2+2^2+3^2}+\ldots$ up to $10^{\text{th}}$ term, is :
questions.key_idea: $T_r=(2r+1)\frac{\sum k^3}{\sum k^2}$ simplifies, with $\sum k^2=\frac{r(r+1)(2r+1)}{6}$, to $\frac{3r(r+1)}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise $T_r=3\binom{r+1}{2}$ and sum with the hockey-stick identity.

useful_results: $\frac{1^3+\ldots+r^3}{1^2+\ldots+r^2}=\frac{3r(r+1)}{2(2r+1)}$, so a factor $(2r+1)$ multiplying it cancels.
Hockey stick: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom{r+1}{2}=\binom{n+2}{3}$; the sum of the first $n$ triangular numbers is the tetrahedral number $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$.
Instance: $n=10$ gives $\frac{10\cdot11\cdot12}6=220$ and $S=3\cdot220=660$.

concepts: Sum of $n$ terms of a series using sums of powers of natural numbers
questions.question: The sum $1+\frac{1^3+2^3}{1+2}+\frac{1^3+2^3+3^3}{1+2+3}+\ldots+\frac{1^3+2^3+3^3+\ldots+15^3}{1+2+3+\ldots+15}-\frac12(1+2+3+\ldots+15)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $\frac{1^3+\cdots+n^3}{1+\cdots+n}=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, a triangular number.

alternate_solutions.idea: The terms are triangular numbers, and the sum of the first $n$ triangular numbers is $\binom{n+2}{3}$.

useful_results: $\frac{\sum k^3}{\sum k}=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ because $\sum k^3=(\sum k)^2$.
The sum of the first $n$ triangular numbers is $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}6$; $n=15$ gives $680$.
The PDF's intermediate values: $\sum n^2=1240$, $\sum n=120$.

concepts: Geometric and arithmetic progressions
questions.question: Let $a,b$ and $c$ be in G.P. with common ratio $r$, where $a\neq0$ and $0<r\le\frac12$. If $3a,7b$ and $15c$ are the first three terms of an A.P., then the $4^{\text{th}}$ term of this A.P. is :
questions.key_idea: Writing $b=ar$, $c=ar^2$, the A.P. condition $14b=3a+15c$ is a quadratic in $r$ whose root $\frac35$ is excluded by $r\le\frac12$.
useful_results: A.P. of three terms: $2\times$ middle $=$ first $+$ last. In an A.P. the fourth term is $2t_3-t_2$; check: $2\cdot\frac{5a}3-\frac{7a}3=a$.
Substituting $r=\frac13$ gives the explicit terms $3a,\frac{7a}{3},\frac{5a}3,a$ (common difference $-\frac{2a}3$).
Constraints on $r$ stated in the problem ($0<r\le\frac12$) are there to reject one root of the quadratic; always apply them.

concepts: Arithmetic progression
Maxima and minima of a cubic polynomial
questions.question: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ be an A.P. with $a_6=2$. Then the common difference of this A.P., which maximises the product $a_1a_4a_5$, is :
questions.key_idea: With $a_6=2$ fixed, $a_1=2-5d$, $a_4=2-2d$, $a_5=2-d$, so the product is a cubic in $d$ whose local maximum (not minimum) is at the larger critical point.
solution: At $d=\frac23$: $\frac{d^2A}{dd^2}=-40+68=28>0$, so $d=\frac23$ is a local minimum (the PDF wrongly writes $<0$).
So the common difference at which the product is maximised (local maximum) is $d=\frac85$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF finds the critical points d = 8/5 and 2/3, then claims 'for d = 2/3, d^2A/dd^2 < 0, hence d = 2/3'. This is wrong: A = -10d^3 + 34d^2 - 32d + 8, A'' = -60d + 68, which is +28 at d = 2/3 (local minimum, A = -32/27) and -28 at d = 8/5 (local maximum, A = 72/25 = 2.88). So the key (A) 2/3 is wrong; the correct answer is (B) 8/5. Note A -> +infinity as d -> -infinity, so 8/5 is the local maximum, which is what the question intends (no global maximum exists).

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor $A'(d)=-2(5d-8)(3d-2)$ and read the sign chart; compare values of $A$ at the critical points.
solution: For $d<\frac23$: both factors negative, product positive, $A'<0$ (A decreasing).
So $A$ falls, rises, then falls: $d=\frac23$ is a local minimum and $d=\frac85$ a local maximum.
Values: $A\left(\frac85\right)=(-6)(-1.2)(0.4)=2.88$ and $A\left(\frac23\right)=\left(-\frac43\right)\left(\frac23\right)\left(\frac43\right)=-\frac{32}{27}$. The answer is $d=\frac85$, option (B).

useful_results: A cubic with negative leading coefficient rises to a local maximum after a local minimum when read left to right: the larger critical point is the local maximum.
Fixing one term of an A.P. ($a_6=2$) lets every other term be written as $2+(k-6)d$: $a_1=2-5d$, $a_4=2-2d$, $a_5=2-d$.
Always test critical points (second derivative or sign chart): a critical point is not automatically the extremum asked for.
A product of three terms of an A.P. is unbounded as $d\to-\infty$, so 'maximises' can only mean a local maximum here.
